name: Esther Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead finish carpenter for a small renovation firm, eight of us, and we do older houses for people with money: staircases, built-in bookcases, kitchens, sash windows. This month I'm rebuilding a curved oak handrail in a hundred-year-old townhouse, and I'm the only one in the firm the owner trusts with it. I get in around half seven, set up my bench in whatever room they've given me, and then it's measuring, scribing and sanding until the light goes. I love the quiet of it and the smell of oak; I hate clients who hover and ask if I've "nearly finished" after an hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the AI tools people talk about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. My boss's daughter Lena does the quotes and the emails on her laptop, and I think she uses something, but I don't go near it. I've got a pencil, a tape, a sliding bevel and thirty-odd chisels, and that's my system. I'm single, I live with my dog Biscuit in a flat above a bakery, and I like my life fairly simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but only to the lads on the van. I'm not one for posting things. Probably I'd just say it to Biscuit, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that's what I want. Nobody's going to get a computer to fit a scribed skirting to a wall that's been leaning since 1920. My work was safe before and it's safe after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Keep working, keep my two or three months of savings topped up, maybe treat myself to the new Japanese plane I've been looking at. I'd be careful with the plane money though, I always am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and pleased. Like getting home and finding the heating's already on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything bother you, even in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that Lena gets faster at quoting and the boss squeezes the timings. He already says "the computer reckons this staircase is four days" and I say the computer's never held a chisel. That would get more annoying, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say back when he says that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I say fine, let the computer come and do it then. He laughs, I do it in six days, and the client's happy. It's a little dance we do.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, but only to the lads in the van, since I don't post things. Mostly I'd say it to my dog Biscuit.
S0.think: For me it means nothing changes, which is what I want. No computer is fitting a scribed skirting to a wall that's been leaning since 1920.
S0.do: Keeps working as before and keeps her two or three months of savings topped up. Perhaps buys the Japanese hand plane she's been eyeing, carefully.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, like coming home to find the heating already on.
S0.quote: He already says "the computer reckons this staircase is four days" and I say the computer's never held a chisel.
S0.fieldNote: Deeply rooted in hand craft and happy for nothing to change. The only friction she imagines is her boss using software estimates to squeeze her timings. Dry humour, private rather than public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be sensible about it, and the ones who lose jobs need help to move into something else. I wouldn't make a fuss. I'd say it over a pint, not on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my sort of work is the last to go in this one. Rich people want an actual person carving their staircase; that's half of what they're paying for. The new-build framers and the office people might have a harder time than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd probably let Lena handle any new software for the firm and stay out of it. If it really came to it, I'd learn one thing, slowly, but I'd wait and see first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of background grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rich people want a person. Is that enough to build a career on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, yes, I think so. There are maybe four people in this city who can do a curved handrail properly and I'm one of them. It's a small pond, but I'm a decent fish in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the boss decided you all had to use some new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him to show me it working on a real job first. I don't want to be the one ruining two hundred pounds of oak because a gadget told me the angle. If it proved itself, I'd use it, grudgingly.

S1.say: I'd say people should be sensible and help those who lose jobs move into something else. I wouldn't make a fuss, and I'd say it over a pint, not online.
S1.think: Honestly I think my work is the last to go: rich clients want a real person carving their staircase. New-build framers and office workers would have it harder.
S1.do: Carries on as she is and leaves any new software to Lena in the office. Waits to see a tool proven on a real job before reluctantly learning it.
S1.feel: Calm, with a bit of background grumbling.
S1.quote: It's a small pond, but I'm a decent fish in it.
S1.fieldNote: She feels shielded by her niche in high-end restoration and by clients who pay for the human touch. Typical of her centre view, she wants sensible help for others but no fuss. Resists tools until proven on real oak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to get on top of it quickly, with something practical, some kind of income for people while things sort out. I don't really know what that looks like. I'd probably keep my head down and not say much in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened, and that's not like me. If a robot can do almost anything as well as a person, then eventually it can scribe a skirting, and my small pond dries up. I'd have about three months saved and no idea what else I'm good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food and Biscuit. No new tools, no holidays, cancel the streaming. I'd take every job going while there were still jobs, weekends too, to stretch the savings to six months. If it got bad I'd ask my brother Marco if I could rent his spare room cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going soft under you. I don't sleep well when things are out of my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't rich clients still want a person, like you said before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few, for a while, the ones who like to show off that a person did it. But if everyone's losing their jobs, even the rich get nervous and stop doing up their houses. And two years isn't long enough for me to find whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn something new in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd even pick. I'm not a computer person, I'm not going to become one at twenty-eight. I'd rather keep my head down, work hard, and hope I'm one of the last ones they still need.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to get on top of it fast with something practical, like an income while things sort out, though I don't know what that looks like. Mostly I'd keep my head down in public.
S2.think: Off the record I'd be frightened, which isn't like me. If a robot can eventually scribe a skirting, my small pond dries up, and I'd have three months saved and no idea what else I'm good for.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and the dog, cancelling streaming, holidays and tool purchases, and takes every job including weekends to stretch savings to six months. Plans to rent her brother Marco's spare room cheaply if things get bad.
S2.feel: Frightened, like the floor going soft, and sleeping badly because things are out of her hands.
S2.quote: If everyone's losing their jobs, even the rich get nervous and stop doing up their houses.
S2.fieldNote: Her confidence rests on one niche, and fast AGI removes it; she also sees the knock-on effect on wealthy clients. She rules out retraining and falls back on frugality and family. Unusually rattled for someone who comes across so self-contained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time, so let's not panic, but let's not pretend either. Sensible planning, help for people to retrain. I'd say it if someone asked me, otherwise I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd see it creeping up. I'd be watching for the first robot that can do decent finish work, and I'd know when that comes I've got maybe a year or two. I'd probably still be in denial right up until then, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and build the savings slowly, maybe from three months to six over the first couple of years. I'd stay where I am, because it's familiar and the boss treats me well. When the robots started on simpler work like doors and skirtings, maybe around 2029, that's when I'd really start thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background, like a noise in the van you keep meaning to get checked. You know it's there, you turn the radio up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be in denial. What would it take to snap you out of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boss losing a big job to a firm with robots, probably. That would make it real. Until money changes hands, it's just stories on Lena's laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years feel compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, but not much. It gives me time to save, not time to become a different person. I'm not sure I want to become a different person.

S3.say: I'd say we've got some time, so let's not panic but let's not pretend either: sensible planning and help to retrain. I'd say it if asked, otherwise keep quiet.
S3.think: Privately I'd watch it creep up and know that once a robot can do decent finish work I'd have a year or two. I'd probably stay in denial until then.
S3.do: Keeps working for the same firm and slowly builds savings from three to six months over two years. Waits until robots start on doors and skirtings, around 2029, before seriously thinking about change.
S3.feel: Anxious in the background, like a noise in the van she keeps meaning to get checked.
S3.quote: It gives me time to save, not time to become a different person. I'm not sure I want to become a different person.
S3.fieldNote: She openly predicts her own denial. Extra time to her means more savings, not change; her resistance to new things is the main barrier. The trigger she names is money lost, not technology seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people are sensible, and the government should use it to get help ready. Honestly, I'd probably not talk about it much. Ten years feels like forever when you're up a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still the same wall, I just hit it at thirty-seven. That's a long time to be good at a trade that's slowly going away. But it's also long enough that I might find my small corner, like restoring listed buildings where the rules say a person has to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and build up the savings, steady, maybe to a year's worth by 2030. I'd try to get onto the heritage work, the old churches and listed houses, because those have strict rules and I think they'd change last. And I'd wait and see what the government sets up, rather than jumping too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slowly. It's a worry that sits there rather than one that grabs you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Heritage work. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I've done two jobs for the heritage people already, a staircase and some window shutters, and they liked me. But I don't know if the rules will stay, nobody knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young person starting out in your trade in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the old ways properly, the hand tools, because that's what's rare. But I'd also tell them to keep a bit of money in the bank. I wouldn't tell them to skip the trade, I couldn't say that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people are sensible, and government should use it to get help ready. I wouldn't talk about it much, since ten years feels like forever up a ladder.
S4.think: Off the record it's the same wall, just at thirty-seven, after a long time in a trade slowly going away. Maybe I'd find a corner in listed buildings where rules say a person must do the work.
S4.do: Keeps working and builds savings steadily towards a year's worth by 2030. Seeks more heritage restoration work on churches and listed houses, and waits to see what support the government sets up.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow way, a worry that sits there rather than one that grabs her.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell them to skip the trade, I couldn't say that.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives her a half-plan, heritage work, built on two real jobs, but she is honest it's partly hope. Even with a decade her approach is to save and wait. Her loyalty to the trade is strong enough that she won't advise young people to avoid it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is some money coming in while I work out what I'm for, some kind of income from the government that doesn't make you feel like a beggar. And maybe rules that keep people on the old buildings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd lose. Not jobs, I mean the know-how. If nobody's carving handrails anymore, in thirty years nobody will know how, and you can't get that back from a computer.

headlineQuote: If nobody's carving handrails anymore, in thirty years nobody will know how, and you can't get that back from a computer.
portrait: Esther is a 27-year-old lead finish carpenter for a small renovation firm, trusted with curved oak handrails and period staircases, who lives alone with her dog above a bakery. She has never used an AI tool and has no wish to; her pencil, bevel and chisels are her system. She is calm in the mild pictures, confident that wealthy clients want a real person. Fast AGI frightens her and she falls back on cutting spending and her brother's spare room; with more time she saves and waits, hoping heritage rules will protect a corner of the trade. She doesn't blame anyone and wants sensible government help, but mostly keeps her head down.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her niche would dry up before she could find anything else she's good for.
whatWouldHelp: A government income that doesn't make her feel like a beggar while she works out what's next, and rules that keep people working on old buildings.
